title: Area VII review: Slow Flight and Stalls
intro: These questions mix all four Tasks of Area VII: slow flight, power-off stalls, power-on stalls and spin awareness. Many link two Tasks, like a stall that turns into a spin.

questions.q: Your trainer's POH lists a 1G stall speed of 53 knots clean and 45 knots with full flaps. The examiner asks for slow flight with full flaps. Which target airspeed best fits the AFH guidance?
options: 47 knots
52 knots
60 knots
65 knots
questions.why: The target is about 5 to 10 knots above the 1G stall speed for that configuration [[24:114|AFH 5-9]] [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. With full flaps that is 50 to 55 knots. 60 knots would fit the clean stall speed, not the full-flap one, and 47 knots is too close to the stall.

questions.q: You are setting up a straight-ahead power-off stall in a trainer with flaps. Which sequence matches the AFH entry?
options: Power to idle first, then lower the nose and extend full flaps at cruise speed to start the descent to the stall
Reduce power and hold altitude to approach speed, set approach attitude and flaps, then power to idle
Pull the nose up to bleed off speed, then extend the flaps and reduce power once the stall horn sounds
Extend full flaps at cruise speed, then reduce power and pull the nose up straight ahead until it stalls
questions.why: The AFH entry: reduce power and hold altitude until you slow to normal approach speed, pitch to the approach attitude, extend the flaps while holding that speed, then set the power to idle. Only then raise the nose to stall [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

questions.q: Look at the figure. Once an airplane is spinning, why does it keep rotating?
options: Both wings are flying normally, and the rudder alone keeps it turning in a flat circle
The rising wing is more stalled, at a higher AOA, with more drag that pulls the airplane around
The descending wing is more stalled, at a higher AOA, with less lift and more drag
The neutral ailerons let the airplane roll freely, so the roll and yaw continue on their own
questions.why: As the airplane rotates, the rising wing is less stalled than the descending wing, which keeps it rolling, yawing and pitching in a spiral [[13:11|AC 61-67C para 107]]. The figure shows the descending wing at a greater AOA, with less lift and more drag [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]. In every spin at least one wing is stalled [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Neutral ailerons are part of the recovery, not the cause [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

questions.q: You are flying a power-on stall at full throttle in a trainer with a fixed-pitch propeller. Which cue may you notice as you near the stall?
options: RPM climbing toward the red line
Controls getting stiffer and quicker to respond
Louder wind noise along the fuselage
A loss of RPM
questions.why: In fixed-pitch propeller airplanes, a loss of RPM may show up as you near a power-on stall. Controls also feel mushy, and the sound of the air along the fuselage usually gets quieter [[13:10|AC 61-67C para 103]].

questions.q: You are in level slow flight right at your target speed. A bump of turbulence knocks off 3 knots, and you don't change pitch or power. What happens?
options: The airspeed keeps dropping, because below L/DMAX the airplane is speed unstable
The airspeed stays 3 knots low but steady
The airspeed comes back to target by itself, because the airplane is trimmed
The airplane climbs, because flying slower makes more lift
questions.why: Below L/DMAX the airplane shows speed instability: after a disturbance the airspeed may keep decaying unless you lower the AOA or add power [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

questions.q: Your airplane is approved for spins in the utility category. Today you have two people in back and bags in the aft compartment, so it is loaded in the normal category. What does the AFH warn?
options: Spins are still fine as long as you stay below VA
The extra weight makes the spin slower and easier to stop
It may not recover from a spin that goes beyond one turn
Only the incipient phase changes; a developed spin is the same
questions.why: An airplane approved for spins in the utility category but loaded in the normal category may not recover from a spin that goes beyond one turn [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. Even a suitcase in the aft baggage area can change spin behavior [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 108]].

questions.q: In a power-off stall recovery you have lowered the nose and leveled the wings. As you add full power, what rudder input does the AFH say may be needed?
options: Full left rudder, to counter P-factor
Left rudder, because the left wing usually stalls first
No rudder, because the ball stays centered by itself as power comes in
Right rudder, to overcome engine torque effects
questions.why: Right rudder pressure may be needed to overcome engine torque effects as power is advanced and the nose is lowered [[24:122|AFH 5-17]]. P-factor also yaws the nose left, so it needs right rudder, not left [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

questions.q: In a power-on stall your right wing drops at the break. You quickly turn the yoke hard left while still holding back pressure. What is the risk?
options: None, because the wing roots stall first and the ailerons keep full effect, so the left roll brings the wing back up
The down aileron on the right wing raises its AOA, deepening the stall there and rolling you further right
The left aileron deflection will pitch the nose up at once and cause an immediate secondary stall of both wings
The left wing will rise so quickly that the horizontal tail stalls and the airplane pitches over into a dive
questions.why: Using aileron before lowering the AOA can make the stall worse: the down aileron on the low wing raises that wing's AOA and stalls the tip more, so the roll can increase. Reduce the AOA first, then roll level [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

questions.q: Use the AFH rule of thumb: the first spin turn loses about 1,000 feet and each later turn loses about half that. A practice stall at 3,000 feet AGL turns into an accidental spin, and the rotation stops after 3 turns. About how high above the ground are you when the rotation stops?
options: 1,000 feet AGL
1,500 feet AGL
2,000 feet AGL
2,500 feet AGL
questions.why: 1,000 + 500 + 500 = 2,000 feet lost, so about 1,000 feet AGL [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]. That is already below the 1,500 feet AGL that spins should be recovered by, before even counting the pullout [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]. This is one reason stalls are practiced high.

questions.q: You practice slow flight in landing configuration over a mountain valley on a hot afternoon, at a much higher density altitude than usual. What should you expect?
options: A higher indicated target speed, because indicated stall speed rises with density altitude
A lower critical AOA, so the wing stalls at a smaller pitch attitude
More engine power available, because the air is thinner
The same indicated target speed, but less engine power available to hold altitude
questions.why: Altitude has little or no effect on indicated stall speed, so the indicated target stays the same [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100j]]. But thin air reduces engine power, propeller thrust and lift [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]], and slow flight already needs high power. The critical AOA does not change with density altitude [[1:124|PHAK 5-27]].

questions.q: On your private pilot checkride, which of these stalls could the examiner ask you to actually fly?
options: A cross-control stall in a skidding turn, as in an overshot base-to-final turn
A secondary stall after a rushed recovery, flown as a full maneuver
A power-off stall from a shallow banked turn (base to final)
An accelerated stall in a 45° bank at or below maneuvering speed
questions.why: Power-off stalls are practiced from shallow banked turns to simulate the base-to-final turn [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. Secondary and cross-control stalls are demonstration-only: only flight instructor applicants may have to perform them. Only commercial and flight instructor applicants may have to perform accelerated stalls [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

questions.q: A power-on stall simulates a departure toward a tall tower. After the recovery, which climb speed gives the most altitude over the shortest distance?
options: VX, best angle of climb
VY, best rate of climb
VA, design maneuvering speed
Your slow flight target speed
questions.why: VX gives the most altitude gain over a given horizontal distance, which is what you want to clear an obstacle. VY gives the most altitude over a given time [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].

questions.q: You fly into unforecast light ice with the autopilot holding altitude, and the airspeed slowly bleeds off. Why does the autopilot make this more dangerous?
options: It adds power by itself to hold altitude, so the airspeed cannot bleed off and a stall cannot develop even in ice
It turns off the stall warning horn while it is engaged, so you get no aural warning until the wing has fully stalled
It lowers the critical AOA of the wing while engaged, so the airplane stalls at a higher indicated airspeed than usual
It may mask stall cues, and a sudden disconnect with controls trimmed to extremes can lead to a spin or spiral
questions.why: The autopilot may mask some of the stall cues you would feel, or try to fly the airplane in the stall. A sudden self-disconnect with the controls trimmed to extreme positions, or out of coordination, can lead to a spin or spiral [[13:10|AC 61-67C para 102c]]. With ice, the stall may also come with little or none of the usual cues [[13:10|AC 61-67C para 102a]].

questions.q: You are in stable, level slow flight. The examiner asks for a straight descent at the same airspeed. What is the right technique?
options: Lower the nose and leave the power where it is
Reduce power, and adjust pitch to hold the target airspeed
Add power and lower the nose
Pull the power to idle and raise the nose to slow the descent
questions.why: Climbs and descents in slow flight are made by adjusting the power [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Below L/DMAX, pitch controls the airspeed and power controls the flightpath [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]. Lowering the nose with the same power would make you speed up.

questions.q: You depart a high airport on a hot afternoon toward rising terrain. You keep raising the nose to climb, the airplane stops climbing, and the stall horn sounds. What should you do?
options: Raise the nose more to trade speed for a little more height and clear the rising terrain
Raise all the flaps at once to cut drag and let the airplane accelerate in the climb
Hold the attitude and wait for the engine to make more power as the airplane keeps climbing
Lower the nose to gain speed, accept some altitude loss, then climb again
questions.why: The stall horn means you are close to the critical AOA, so first lower the AOA [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. The AFH's hot, high departure example teaches the same idea: the fix is not intuitive. Gain speed at the cost of some altitude, then climb again once the airplane has excess power [[24:101|AFH 4-15]] [[24:102|AFH 4-16]]. Raising the nose more only bleeds more speed.

questions.q: In a power-off stall recovery, a student keeps the nose low long after the stall warning stops, and the airspeed races toward the red line. What is the problem?
options: Nothing; more airspeed always makes the recovery safer
A secondary stall, because the nose was lowered too far
Too much airspeed buildup; the airspeed should never reach the red line in a practice stall
A spin, because the wings were leveled
questions.why: Excessive airspeed buildup during recovery is a common stall error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. The airspeed indicator or tachometer should never reach its red line during a practice stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C para 105]].

questions.q: A full-flap power-off stall goes wrong at altitude and the airplane enters a spin. Besides the normal spin recovery steps, what does the AFH say about the flaps?
options: Extend them fully if they were only partly down
Leave them down, because they lower the stall speed and help the recovery
Retract them as soon as practicable after spin entry
Leave them down until you are back in level flight, then raise them all at once
questions.why: If the flaps or retractable gear are extended before the spin, they should be retracted as soon as practicable after spin entry [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

questions.q: How do the stall cues in a power-on stall compare with a power-off stall?
options: They are the same in every way
Power-on cues are weaker; the main cue is the elevator against its stop
A power-on stall gives no buffet, only the horn
Buffeting and shaking are more noticeable in the power-on stall
questions.why: In a power-off stall the cues (buffeting, shaking) are less noticeable than in a power-on stall. In a power-off 1G stall, the main cue may be the elevator full aft against the stops and a high descent rate [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

questions.q: In slow flight the nose is high and you are busy with power and rudder. How should you scan for traffic?
options: One quick sweep across the whole windshield every few minutes, then back to the instruments
Short eye movements of 10° or less, looking at each area at least 1 second
Keep your eyes on the instruments and wait for ATC to call out any traffic near you
Look only straight ahead, since the high nose blocks your view of the sides and traffic
questions.why: Effective scanning uses short, regularly spaced eye movements of no more than 10 degrees, with each area watched for at least 1 second [[24:32|AFH 1-11]]. Clear the area before the maneuver too [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

questions.q: Your engine quits and you are a little short of the only good field. Which action does the straight-ahead power-off stall train you to avoid?
options: Raising the nose to stretch the glide
Picking a closer field
Leaving the flaps up until the field is made
Lowering the nose to hold best glide speed
questions.why: The power-off straight-ahead stall simulates the stall that can happen when a pilot tries to stretch a glide after an engine failure, or is low on the approach [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

questions.q: Which situation does AC 61-67C call a classic case where P-factor can play a big role in a stall/spin accident?
options: Cruise flight at low power in smooth air with the airplane trimmed for level flight
A go-around or short-field takeoff: high pitch, power and low airspeed
A power-off glide at best glide speed with the airplane trimmed in a steady descent
A shallow descent at high airspeed with the power at idle and the nose well below the horizon
questions.why: At high AOA and high power, P-factor yaws the airplane left. Too little or too much rudder makes the flight uncoordinated, and in a go-around or short-field takeoff that can lead to a stall/spin [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]].

questions.q: With no POH spin procedure, why does the generic spin recovery start with power to idle?
options: Power aggravates a spin: it can flatten the spin and usually speeds up the rotation
Idle power lets you hold the elevator full aft during the recovery
Idle power raises the critical AOA so the wing unstalls
Idle power makes the turn indicator show the spin direction
questions.why: Power aggravates spin characteristics. It can make the spin flatter and usually increases the rate of rotation [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

questions.q: During a power-off stall, which sign tells you the wing has reached a full stall, not just an impending stall?
options: The stall horn first sounds
Light buffeting begins
The nose pitches down by itself and you can't readily stop it
The controls start to feel mushy
questions.why: An impending stall gives warnings such as buffeting, a stick shaker or an aural warning before the critical AOA. A full stall is usually an uncommanded nose-down pitch that can't be readily stopped, maybe with a roll [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

questions.q: You are done with slow flight in landing configuration and want to return to cruise at the same altitude. Which exit matches the AFH?
options: Add power, then use forward pressure to hold altitude, and clean up flaps and gear as speed builds
Lower the nose first to gain speed, then add power once airspeed is up and raise all the flaps and gear at once
Raise all the flaps at once to cut drag, then add power as the airplane accelerates and hold altitude
Reduce power and dive to gain speed quickly, then level off at cruise altitude and retract the flaps and gear
questions.why: To exit, add power. As airspeed and lift increase, use forward pressure to hold altitude, stay coordinated, then retract flaps and gear as speed increases and retrim [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Raising the flaps abruptly in slow flight can stall the airplane [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].
